ACUTE STROKE Patients on antiplatelet or antithrombotic therapy19 and their sudden discontinuation, patients with carotid bruit, patients with prior history of stroke, patients with cardiovascular disease are all at potential risk for stroke.18 Pre-procedural evaluation by a physician or a neurologist has to be considered in such patients. During the procedure, the dermatologist’s role chiefly concerns the detection phase of a sudden neurologic deficit. This may include an alteration in consciousness (confusion, coma and seizures), aphasia, dysarthria, facial weakness or asymmetry, extremity weakness, paralysis, sensory loss, ataxia, visual loss or vertigo. Immediately activate the physician or emergency medical services. A definitive hospital-based intervention must occur within 3 hours of the onset of the stroke symptoms to be beneficial. Meanwhile attend to the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) of resuscitation and monitor vitals and manage accordingly till the physician arrives.
STATUS EPILEPTICUS Dermatologists do encounter disease with potential epileptic manifestations in conditions such as tuberous sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (Box 5). It is wise to obtain any past history of seizures and antiseizure medications.20 If the patients are epileptic on treatment, one should advise them to continue the treatment until the day of surgery. Box 5: Management of status epilepticus. • Stop the ongoing procedure. First priority is always the maintenance of airway. Use an oral or naso­pharyn­geal airway as and when required (inserting these airways are out of the routine for dermatological surgeons, it is advisable for them to learn the insertion of these airways from their anesthesia or critical care colleagues) • If available, oxygen can be delivered by face mask • Monitor the vital signs • Place the patient on a soft, flat surface away from sharp objects • Look for and prevent tongue bite • If seizures has stopped and the patient is breathing and has a pulse, place the patient in a recovery position (modified lateral position).It will allow the clearance of any pooled secretions • Secure a peripheral intravenous line and send blood sample for blood glucose, serum electrolytes • The benzodiazepine midazolam or lorazepam 1–2 mg or diazepam 5–10 mg intravenously will stop the seizures • Call for physician and evaluate for seizures etiology and further management options

COLLAPSE Most commonly syncope, anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia and cardiac arrest are reasons for collapse of a patient. These issues may be addressed as discussed in the chapter. However, associated with a vasomotor collapse are some of the key issues mentioned below which need attention.
HYPOTENSION Low blood pressure may result from bleeding, syncope, anaphylaxis, acute myocardial infarction, and secondary to medications such as sedatives/anesthetic agents. Patient may complain of giddiness (or orthostatic hypotension).
Management Place the patient in supine position and check vital signs such as, pulse rate and blood pressure. Treat the underlying cause. Tachycardia with low blood pressure indicates blood loss, start the patient on intravenous fluid crystalloids. Ringer’s lactate 5–10 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes can be administered and the blood pressure checked. If good response continues, intravenous fluid (Ringer’s lactate) at the rate of 2–4 mL/kg/hour may be continued. If there is no response to the fluids, check for continued blood loss; send a sample of blood for checking the hemoglobin level. In the absence of matched donor blood, it is vital to maintain the circulating blood volume by administration of colloids such as starch solutions. More damage might be caused by allowing hypovolemia than anemia.21,22 If hypotension persists, one should seek a physician’s opinion and have a provision for starting an inotropic infusion such as injection dopamine 5 µg/kg/ min should be commenced.
HYPERTENSION Known hypertensives, elderly, female, anxious patients are prone for increased blood pressure during the procedure. Accelerated hypertensive patients can also present with giddiness, severe headache. Optimization of blood pressure for known hypertensives, reassuring the patients, premedicant such as alprazolam, sedatives such as midazolam, lorazepam would help in the control of blood pressure. Involvement of a physician would be helpful if basic interventions do not reduce the blood pressure.

Dermatological Procedures and Infection Control Infections after dermatological procedures are not only rare but usually insignificant. These procedures are majorly aesthetic ones and these ‘patients’ do not suffer from any major systemic illnesses; the expectation about outcomes are usually high. Absence of infection after the procedure is one such expectation. The dermatologic surgeon must attend to the infection control measures in providing clean

texts.418: Section 1: Basic Principles of Cutaneous Surgery ambience while conducting the procedure, using standard precautions, preoperative decolonization of methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and surgical prophylaxis. Postprocedure, the patients may be advised about care of the wound and reporting early if signs of infection come up. Preoperative preparation: It is a common knowledge that Staphylococcus aureus is a common cutaneous com­ mensal; it is impossible to eradicate it. While conducting surgical operations requiring skin incision, the colony count of these organisms have to be reduced. The methods to achieve this are: a. Preoperative chlorhexidine 2% v/v wash: The patients have to bathe twice daily for 3 preoperative days. This solution cannot be applied over the scalp and face. Those wishing to operate on the scalp and the face may use triclosan solution. b. Intranasal mupirocin ointment: All the surgical patients must be requested to use mupirocin ointment twice daily for 5 days preoperatively. This decolonizes the nasal mucosa of MRSA. c. Surgical preparation: It is recommended that we must use chlorhexidine tincture 2% w/v to prepare the skin. This solution has been found to be superior to using povidone iodine; its residual action is longer than that of povidone iodine. Whether chlorhexidine or povidone iodine is used, one must wait for at least 3 minutes prior to incision. The commonly found practice of ‘rubbing off’ excess solution using a gauze should be shunned and instead, the solution must be allowed to dry by itself; only then the antibacterial effect is maximized. d. Preoperative surgical prophylaxis: It is recommended by Center for Disease Control and Prevention that a single dose of first or second generation cephalosporin be administered intravenously 15–60 minutes prior to incision. Administering 1.5 g of cefuroxime suffices in most adults. If the surgery continues beyond 4 hours, a similar dose must be administered. e. Normoglycemia and normothermia: It has been shown that intraoperative blood sugar and temperature maintenance is absolutely essential. Cutaneous surgeries are no exception to these recommendations.

HYPOXEMIA Patient developing desaturation during the procedure requires attention. Hypoxemia may be secondary to pain induced hypoventilation, pulmonary embolism (during lipo­suction), cardiac failure, bronchospasm due to anaphylaxis.

Stop the procedure and start oxygen by face mask, 4 L/ minute. Talk to the patient and encourage them to breathe deeply. Assess the vitals, talk to the patient. Reassure him. Determine the underlying cause. Notify the physician. Treat the underlying cause.
CARDIAC ARREST7,23 The most common cause of cardiac arrest is ventricular fibrillation, other arrhythmias like pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity also lead to cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest is confirmed when the patient is not responding, pulse is not felt, blood pressure is not recor­ dable. Immediate measures to be taken are: zz Activate the emergency department/notify the physician or an anesthesiologist. zz Start cardiopulmonary resuscitation as per American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines 2010.23 zz Start chest compression at the rate of 100/minute. zz Get an automated external defibrillator device. Diagnose ventricular fibrillation and defibrillate. zz Continue chest compressions. zz Begin ventilation. zz Administer oxygen. zz Obtain intravenous access. zz Administer epinephrine or vasopressin. zz Assess adequacy of Clinical Practice Redesign efforts. zz Intubate trachea. zz Additional drug therapy. zz Post-resuscitation care and shift of the patient to a higher medical center for further management.
NERVE INJURY Inadvertent nerve damage is one of the most dreaded complications of dermatologic surgery. Effects of local anesthesia, inadvertent pressure or tension due to posi­ tioning are the common cause. Nerve injuries may result in transient either reversible or permanent. Patients should always be warned of the possibility of nerve injury during the discussion of the informed consent. Patient should be frequently asked about any discomfort induced by prolonged positioning.

Differential diagnosis: Find and treat the reversible causes for cardiac arrest, which is easily remembered in a mnemonic form as 5 Hs and 5 Ts. –– Hs: Hypovolemia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hyper/ hypokalemia, hypoglycemia, hypothermia. –– Ts: Toxins, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, thrombosis (coronary and pulmonary), trauma. General supportive care of the patient and specific pharmacologic therapy aimed at underlying event causing cardiac arrest should be initiated once the patient is successfully resuscitated.
DOCUMENTATION OF THE EVENTS All adverse events and the measures taken are to be documented, discussed with the patient, and a discharge summary of the event to be issued to the patient. The exact time of the event may not be relevant but the flow of events and their management may be important. Such documentations are important from the medicolegal view point too. There are certain tips given for the avoidance of complications in Box 7.

CONCLUSION Complications in dermatosurgery office based-procedures although rare, do occur, and the outcomes of such events are related to the initial diagnosis and early management. Thorough preprocedural evaluation and identification of high-risk patients, 24 optimization of coexisting medical illness with medications will go a long way in preventing adverse events during the procedure. Good communication and patient rapport are important. Highrisk cases, technologically advanced procedures should be scheduled under monitored anesthesia care and in a hospital with full-fledged emergency backup facility. A well-planned and organized office setup under the leadership of a dermato­logist proves to be beneficial to the patients and reduce the medicolegal complications too.

Though dermatosurgeries are office procedures, surgical emergencies may occur, though they are rare. Dermatological surgeons should be fully aware of procedures for resuscitation in such eventualities. Syncope, bleeding and issues concerning lignocaine use are the common events that might occur. Monitoring devices, basic resuscitation equipments, adequate trained staff are needed to manage an emergency. The adage “If you are prepared for an emergency, it ceases to exist” appears to be apt under these situations.
INTRODUCTION Office-based dermatologic procedures and cosmetic surgeries performed on a day care basis have become the trend of the day. Such procedures are supported by anesthesiologists at certain centers and by resident doctors or nurses at others. The support provided by the anesthesiologists in these situations is referred to as “Monitored Anesthesia Care”.1 Complications, though uncommon, have been reported in 6% of such procedures: bleeding or hematoma in 3%, infections in 2% and vasovagal reactions in 1%. Bleeding occurred more frequently in menor in patients taking anticoagulation, antiplatelet or immunosuppressive agents or in; in prolonged procedures. Vasovagal reactions were associated with age younger than 50 years.2,3 The preparedness of the dermatologists in dealing with such crises affects the outcome of the situation. With the society getting more and more litingant, it is time that dermatologists attend to quality and safety issues while dealing with these "patients", who do not usually suffer from disease. The emphasis is on the patient safety and adequate infra­structure to deal with the complications that may arise during the procedure. Availability of the monitoring devices, basic resuscitation equipments, adequate trained staff and the ability to manage an emergency should be always borne in mind of the dermatologic surgeons prior to starting the scheduled procedure at the office.4,5 It may be misconceived by a few dermatologic surgeons that complications are rare and therefore the therapeutic agents

and knowledge to deal with the crises at their office may not be required. Providing infrastructural support to deal with crises in day care surgery not only makes the day care procedures safer for the patient, but also avoids potential medicolegal complications. This chapter discusses the spectrum of emergencies that are commonly encountered by the dermatosurgeon and the basic guidelines to manage these emergency situations. Dermatologic surgery is mostly cosmetic; therefore, the potential for medicolegal issues is high in the event of adverse outcome. In the author’s view, the entire team in the dermatologic surgeon’s procedure room should be trained to provide at least basic life support (BLS), if not advanced cardiac life support (ACLS). Dermatologic surgeons need to practice and adopt “Safe surgery saves lives” campaign as proposed by World Health Organization.6 A few of the points for safe surgery are mentioned in Box 1. Several emergency issues may be encountered in the practice of surgical dermatology.7 These are illustrated in Box 2.
ANAPHYLAXIS Anaphylaxis is a sudden violent manifestation of an acute immunological reaction, which might become life threatening at times. It is produced by a complex mec­ hanism involving the immune system. The manifestation may vary from pruritus, urticarial in milder cases and inspiratory stridor, laryngeal edema, bronchospasm,

Other fluids such as dextrose and saline may be infused depending on the requirement • In diabetic patients check the blood sugar by ‘glucostrip’ method • Connect electrocardiogram and pulse oximetry in all the patients. If access to chest is difficult to obtain, loose fitting clothes allowing access to chest may be worn • Prepare the local anesthetic infiltration yourself. It has been shown that presence of a professional watching the patient’s vitals improves the detection of anaphylaxis and its treatment.8 Common causes of such anaphylaxis in a dermatologic practice are adverse reactions to intravenous antibiotic

Anaphylaxis Syncope Lignocaine-related issues Breathlessness Chest pain Bleeding Acute stroke Status epilepticus Hypotension Hypoxia Cardiac arrest
Box 4: Tips for avoiding syncopal attacks. • Explaining the patient about the procedure and allaying anxiety often helps in reducing the incidence of syncope as also performing the procedures in a supine position • Shielding the eyes and placing a surgical sheet to block the patient view from the operated area may help prevent the occurrence of syncope. A distracting conversation may be beneficial • Following the procedure, the patient should slowly sit up and be observed for several minutes while postoperative instructions are being discussed. Sitting up suddenly and standing immediately after the procedure could also result in syncope after the completion of the procedure.11
agents, local anesthetic agents and other allergens such as latex rubber. Box 3 shows management of anaphylaxis. Anaphylactoid reactions are similar but are not immuno­logically mediated. They may be prevented by prior administration of corticosteroids and antihistaminic agents. These are common subsequent to administration of radiological ionic dyes and a few anesthetic agents such as atracurium and suxamethonium which are likely to release histamine.10 However, these are not common in dermatosurgical practice.
SYNCOPE Syncope is a vagal-mediated unconsciousness, commonly associated with extreme bradycardia and at times pulseless states. It is commonly encountered in anxious patients. It is often confused with anaphylaxis, if it occurs after an injection. Starting of an intravenous cannulation, surgical incision in inadequately anesthetized areas and even sight of blood might trigger it. An early sign of syncope, prior to loss of consciousness, is profuse sweating and cold skin. Vagal-induced bradycardia in the setting of decreased systemic vascular resistance can initiate collapse. Pseudoseizure activity may occur, characterized by brief clonic activity. Blood pressure may initially decrease but is restored with supine position. The tips for avoiding syncopal attacks are mentioned in Box 4.
Management of Syncope Place the patient in supine and preferably in a head down (Trendelenburg) position. Monitor vital parameters such
237
238

Section 1: Basic Principles of Cutaneous Surgery as heart rate, blood pressure and pulse oximetry. Reassure the patient; that may all be necessary in addition to the recumbent posture. Start intravenous access. Administer injection atropine 1 mg if heart rate is less than 40 per minute and intravenous fluids if blood pressure continues to be low. If alone, one should call for help and step up the monitoring only after minimal monitoring has been started to begin with.
LIGNOCAINE-RELATED ISSUES Patients with multiple allergies and atopy are more likely to develop lignocaine allergy.12 Most of the adverse reactions that are clinically seen are in fact manifestation of the over dosage of the local anesthetic by inadvertent intravascular injection in extremely vascular areas such as the scalp and face. It can also occur in cases of tumescent liposuction when dosages over 55 mg/kg are used. In such cases, signs of over dosage are often delayed. A case of lignocaine over dosage leading to death late at mid night, after liposuction has recently been reported.13 Toxic reactions to lignocaine resulting from over dosage cause central nervous system or myocardial depression or excitation, perioral numbness, nausea, seizures or coma. Vasovagal syncope may be misdiagnosed as an allergic reaction and should be distinguished properly. Methylparaben and propylparaben are the preservatives added to lignocaine and various cosmetics to increase their shelf life. Some of the adverse reactions seen during administration of lignocaine may indeed be due to these preservatives.14 Patients who are allergic to sulfa drugs may develop adverse reactions to ‘sulfites’ which are added as preservatives to lignocaine. Anxiety regarding the use of needles, and/or the effects of epinephrine in lignocaine can lead to palpitations, panic attacks and vasovagal events that the patient may remember as an allergic reaction. Patients admitting to having had previous incorrectly allergic reactions should be properly investiga­ ted prior to submitting for dermatologic surgery. The dermatologic surgical procedure in patients with allergic manifestations may be electively performed under general anesthesia and management of such cases in a hospital with a full back up should be planned.15 More information on local anesthetics and their allergic reactions is provided in the chapter on Local Anesthesia in Dermatosurgery.

BREATHLESSNESS The etiologies of breathlessness may be cardiac, respiratory or anxiety related. Patients with asthma and obstructive airway disease should be well investigated by a pulmonologist and rendered ‘dry’ before scheduling for dermatologic surgery. Such patients should be advised to use the routine inhalers before arriving for surgery.16 Dermatologic surgeons should also check the preoperative ‘basal’ values of oxygen and carbon dioxide. In the absence of this knowledge one may treat in vain to achieve magic
numbers of partial pressures of more than 100 mm Hg and carbon dioxide of less than 40. Patients with ‘cardiac asthma’ should be well prepared with diuretic and peripheral vasodilator therapy. At times cardiac patients manifest with dyspnea when subjected to myocardial ischemia. Even young obese individuals might present with dyspnea of cardiac origin. Patients with respiratory compromise should not be operated without the guidance of pulse oximetry. If the oxygen saturation decreases during surgery, methods to administer the bronchodilator nebulization must be kept handy. Dyspnea which does not abate with treatment, whether of cardiac or pulmonary origin is a reason to stop the scheduled procedure and to reschedule at a later convenient time. Dyspnea due to anxiety will respond well to a small intravenous dose (0.5–1 mg) of anxiolytic such as midazolam. Appropriate preoperative counseling is sufficient in most patients to avoid anxiety related problems.

CHEST PAIN Chest pain may be a manifestation of not only coronary arterial ischemia but also anxiety. However, fear, stress of pain and procedure can also precipitate an acute myocardial infarction in any patient prone for ischemia. Although most dermatologic surgical procedures are day care and performed in young healthy individuals, at times, if a high-risk patient is being subjected to esthetic surgery, thorough evaluation would be mandatory. If a patient complains of chest pain during the procedure, place the patient supine and check the vitals. Activate physician/emergency medical services. Record an electrocardiogram, which may be compared against the basal. If you are suspecting coronary ischemia, a tablet of nitroglycerine 5 mg should be placed immediately under the tongue. One must be aware of possible headache and hypotension following this measure. An intravenous (IV) cannula should be inserted immediately (if not already done) and a patent IV line is important for further management. If with these measures the chest pain settles and the patient is hemodynamically stable, one can proceed with the surgery. If the pain is unabated and electro­cardiographic changes persist or worsen, the scheduled procedure should be deferred with. Patient may undergo the scheduled procedure after a consult with a cardiologist. Patients at risk for myocardial ischemia should be thoroughly evaluated and medically optimized prior to the procedure. In the author’s opinion, it may be wise to have ‘monitored anesthesia care’ for all patients.
BLEEDING A major surgical bleeder is rare in cutaneous surgeries. A patient receiving antiplatelet medications for concomitant comorbidities may pose special issues. Such patients may be better prepared by stopping the antiplatelet medication
Chapter 18: Management of Dermatosurgical Emergencies at least for 2 weeks prior to the planned procedure. Although the hemorrhage associated with cutaneous surgery may not be life threatening, its other effects such as causing a menacing hematoma and lifting of flaps compromising their viability may be of nuisance value.17,18 For more information on hemostasis reader is referred to the chapter on Hemostasis.

ACUTE STROKE Patients on antiplatelet or antithrombotic therapy19 and their sudden discontinuation, patients with carotid bruit, patients with prior history of stroke, patients with cardiovascular disease are all at potential risk for stroke.18 Pre-procedural evaluation by a physician or a neurologist has to be considered in such patients. During the procedure, the dermatologist’s role chiefly concerns the detection phase of a sudden neurologic deficit. This may include an alteration in consciousness (confusion, coma and seizures), aphasia, dysarthria, facial weakness or asymmetry, extremity weakness, paralysis, sensory loss, ataxia, visual loss or vertigo. Immediately activate the physician or emergency medical services. A definitive hospital-based intervention must occur within 3 hours of the onset of the stroke symptoms to be beneficial. Meanwhile attend to the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) of resuscitation and monitor vitals and manage accordingly till the physician arrives.
STATUS EPILEPTICUS Dermatologists do encounter disease with potential epileptic manifestations in conditions such as tuberous sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (Box 5). It is wise to obtain any past history of seizures and antiseizure medications.20 If the patients are epileptic on treatment, one should advise them to continue the treatment until the day of surgery. Box 5: Management of status epilepticus. • Stop the ongoing procedure. First priority is always the maintenance of airway. Use an oral or naso­pharyn­geal airway as and when required (inserting these airways are out of the routine for dermatological surgeons, it is advisable for them to learn the insertion of these airways from their anesthesia or critical care colleagues) • If available, oxygen can be delivered by face mask • Monitor the vital signs • Place the patient on a soft, flat surface away from sharp objects • Look for and prevent tongue bite • If seizures has stopped and the patient is breathing and has a pulse, place the patient in a recovery position (modified lateral position).It will allow the clearance of any pooled secretions • Secure a peripheral intravenous line and send blood sample for blood glucose, serum electrolytes • The benzodiazepine midazolam or lorazepam 1–2 mg or diazepam 5–10 mg intravenously will stop the seizures • Call for physician and evaluate for seizures etiology and further management options

COLLAPSE Most commonly syncope, anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia and cardiac arrest are reasons for collapse of a patient. These issues may be addressed as discussed in the chapter. However, associated with a vasomotor collapse are some of the key issues mentioned below which need attention.
HYPOTENSION Low blood pressure may result from bleeding, syncope, anaphylaxis, acute myocardial infarction, and secondary to medications such as sedatives/anesthetic agents. Patient may complain of giddiness (or orthostatic hypotension).
Management Place the patient in supine position and check vital signs such as, pulse rate and blood pressure. Treat the underlying cause. Tachycardia with low blood pressure indicates blood loss, start the patient on intravenous fluid crystalloids. Ringer’s lactate 5–10 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes can be administered and the blood pressure checked. If good response continues, intravenous fluid (Ringer’s lactate) at the rate of 2–4 mL/kg/hour may be continued. If there is no response to the fluids, check for continued blood loss; send a sample of blood for checking the hemoglobin level. In the absence of matched donor blood, it is vital to maintain the circulating blood volume by administration of colloids such as starch solutions. More damage might be caused by allowing hypovolemia than anemia.21,22 If hypotension persists, one should seek a physician’s opinion and have a provision for starting an inotropic infusion such as injection dopamine 5 µg/kg/ min should be commenced.
HYPERTENSION Known hypertensives, elderly, female, anxious patients are prone for increased blood pressure during the procedure. Accelerated hypertensive patients can also present with giddiness, severe headache. Optimization of blood pressure for known hypertensives, reassuring the patients, premedicant such as alprazolam, sedatives such as midazolam, lorazepam would help in the control of blood pressure. Involvement of a physician would be helpful if basic interventions do not reduce the blood pressure.

Dermatological Procedures and Infection Control Infections after dermatological procedures are not only rare but usually insignificant. These procedures are majorly aesthetic ones and these ‘patients’ do not suffer from any major systemic illnesses; the expectation about outcomes are usually high. Absence of infection after the procedure is one such expectation. The dermatologic surgeon must attend to the infection control measures in providing clean
239
240

Section 1: Basic Principles of Cutaneous Surgery ambience while conducting the procedure, using standard precautions, preoperative decolonization of methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and surgical prophylaxis. Postprocedure, the patients may be advised about care of the wound and reporting early if signs of infection come up. Preoperative preparation: It is a common knowledge that Staphylococcus aureus is a common cutaneous com­ mensal; it is impossible to eradicate it. While conducting surgical operations requiring skin incision, the colony count of these organisms have to be reduced. The methods to achieve this are: a. Preoperative chlorhexidine 2% v/v wash: The patients have to bathe twice daily for 3 preoperative days. This solution cannot be applied over the scalp and face. Those wishing to operate on the scalp and the face may use triclosan solution. b. Intranasal mupirocin ointment: All the surgical patients must be requested to use mupirocin ointment twice daily for 5 days preoperatively. This decolonizes the nasal mucosa of MRSA. c. Surgical preparation: It is recommended that we must use chlorhexidine tincture 2% w/v to prepare the skin. This solution has been found to be superior to using povidone iodine; its residual action is longer than that of povidone iodine. Whether chlorhexidine or povidone iodine is used, one must wait for at least 3 minutes prior to incision. The commonly found practice of ‘rubbing off’ excess solution using a gauze should be shunned and instead, the solution must be allowed to dry by itself; only then the antibacterial effect is maximized. d. Preoperative surgical prophylaxis: It is recommended by Center for Disease Control and Prevention that a single dose of first or second generation cephalosporin be administered intravenously 15–60 minutes prior to incision. Administering 1.5 g of cefuroxime suffices in most adults. If the surgery continues beyond 4 hours, a similar dose must be administered. e. Normoglycemia and normothermia: It has been shown that intraoperative blood sugar and temperature maintenance is absolutely essential. Cutaneous surgeries are no exception to these recommendations.

HYPOXEMIA Patient developing desaturation during the procedure requires attention. Hypoxemia may be secondary to pain induced hypoventilation, pulmonary embolism (during lipo­suction), cardiac failure, bronchospasm due to anaphylaxis.
Management The management steps of hypoxemia are mentioned below:

Stop the procedure and start oxygen by face mask, 4 L/ minute. Talk to the patient and encourage them to breathe deeply. Assess the vitals, talk to the patient. Reassure him. Determine the underlying cause. Notify the physician. Treat the underlying cause.
CARDIAC ARREST7,23 The most common cause of cardiac arrest is ventricular fibrillation, other arrhythmias like pulseless ventricular tachycardia, pulseless electrical activity also lead to cardiac arrest. Cardiac arrest is confirmed when the patient is not responding, pulse is not felt, blood pressure is not recor­ dable. Immediate measures to be taken are: zz Activate the emergency department/notify the physician or an anesthesiologist. zz Start cardiopulmonary resuscitation as per American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines 2010.23 zz Start chest compression at the rate of 100/minute. zz Get an automated external defibrillator device. Diagnose ventricular fibrillation and defibrillate. zz Continue chest compressions. zz Begin ventilation. zz Administer oxygen. zz Obtain intravenous access. zz Administer epinephrine or vasopressin. zz Assess adequacy of Clinical Practice Redesign efforts. zz Intubate trachea. zz Additional drug therapy. zz Post-resuscitation care and shift of the patient to a higher medical center for further management.
NERVE INJURY Inadvertent nerve damage is one of the most dreaded complications of dermatologic surgery. Effects of local anesthesia, inadvertent pressure or tension due to posi­ tioning are the common cause. Nerve injuries may result in transient either reversible or permanent. Patients should always be warned of the possibility of nerve injury during the discussion of the informed consent. Patient should be frequently asked about any discomfort induced by prolonged positioning.

GENERAL RESUSCITATION PLAN AT THE DERMATOLOGIC OFFICE Training of each and every staff member at the dermato­ logic office with clearly defined roles for each staff is a must in managing an emergency scenario (Box 6). Preferably, an anesthetist should be available on the premises, particularly when surgeries such as liposuction

are being performed. In his absence, a person trained in ACLS should be available. Various roles played by the staff members can be practiced several times so that they can act accordingly in an emergency situation. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) training which includes BLS and ACLS are conducted by various health organizations in accordance with AHA. All the staff members should undergo the BLS course whereas the dermatosurgeon/team leader or the nursing staff should undergo both BLS and ACLS course.

LIST OF RESUSCITATION EQUIPMENT The basic resuscitation equipments in the form of crash cart should be made available in each dermatologist’s office (Fig. 1): Telephone remains the most important piece of emergency equipment in the dermatosurgeon’s office; it provides the first link in the chain of initiating the emergency medical services process. Crash cart should comprise of: Portable oxygen cylinder with face mask or nasal prongs, oral or nasopharyngeal airways, intravenous cannulas, tubings, fluids and suction apparatus. zz Medications: Epinephrine 1:1,000, lorazepam, diazepam, diphenhydramine, dextrose 50%, nitro­ glycerine tablets, baby aspirin. zz Automated external defibrillators (AED) are comp­ uterized devices consisting of adhesive electrodes which recognize cardiac rhythms and deliver an electrical shock across the chest wall to terminate the ventricular fibrillation. They are portable and user friendly. Adhesive electrodes are placed over the patient’s cardiac apex and upper right chest to detect the cardiac rhythm. With audible and visual prompting, the device advises the operator to press the button and deliver a defibrillating shock. zz Laryngoscope, endotracheal tubes, AMBU bag. zz The crash cart inventory should be periodically reviewed and renewed as necessary. zz Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is a life-saving measure which supports pumping of blood by the heart thus zz

allowing oxygen to reach the brain. It is more effective when done as early as possible. The conduct of CPR is guided by AHA guidelines recently updated in 2010.23 zz Cardiopulmonary resuscitation includes recognition of cardiac arrest, activating emergency medical services (EMS), and to get an AED, performing BLS and ACLS. zz Components of BLS: The primary survey “circulation airway breathing”. zz Circulation: Chest compression keeps the blood pumping to the vital organs. It is done at the rate of 100 compressions per minute, at an adequate depth of 2–2.5 inches, and allowing complete chest recoil. zz Airway and breathing: Opening the patient’s airway by performing the head tilt chin lift, and give breath by mask-mouth. Chest compression to ventilation ratio is 30:2. zz Defibrillation: Once the AED arrives, switch on the defibrillator; attach the adhesive electrodes to the patient’s chest. Clear the patient and once the defibril­ lator analyzes the rhythm, follow the defibrillators instructions. All the medic and paramedic staff members in the dermatology setup should be trained in performing the BLS, performing the chest compressions, maintaining the airway, handling the AED. Components of ACLS: The Secondary Survey Circulation: Obtain intravenous access, attach ECG leads and monitor for arrhythmias or cardiac arrest. Use of drugs/IV fluids to manage rhythm and blood pressure. zz Airway: Maintain the airway patency—use of airways, advanced airway management if needed using a laryngeal masks airway/endotracheal tube. zz Breathing: Give supplemental oxygen; assess the adequacy of ventilation by noting the chest rise, oxygen saturation, capnography (expired carbon dioxide measurement). zz

Section 1: Basic Principles of Cutaneous Surgery Box 7: Tips for avoidance of complications. • Thorough preoperative evaluation, optimal manage­ment of the coexisting medical illness24 • Preprocedural counseling, premedication to allay anxiety. Explanation in detail the procedure, postprocedural care • Basic monitoring facilities: Pulse oximetry, non­invasive blood pressure, electrocardiogram should be made available • Avoidance of drugs which has previously caused reactions • Involvement of anesthesiologist (Standby anesthesiologists to provide monitored anesthesia care) as and when required, at the earliest and discussion of various anesthetic options available in the conduct of safe procedure • Establishment of clear postprocedural instructions

Differential diagnosis: Find and treat the reversible causes for cardiac arrest, which is easily remembered in a mnemonic form as 5 Hs and 5 Ts. –– Hs: Hypovolemia, hydrogen ion (acidosis), hyper/ hypokalemia, hypoglycemia, hypothermia. –– Ts: Toxins, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, thrombosis (coronary and pulmonary), trauma. General supportive care of the patient and specific pharmacologic therapy aimed at underlying event causing cardiac arrest should be initiated once the patient is successfully resuscitated.
DOCUMENTATION OF THE EVENTS All adverse events and the measures taken are to be documented, discussed with the patient, and a discharge summary of the event to be issued to the patient. The exact time of the event may not be relevant but the flow of events and their management may be important. Such documentations are important from the medicolegal view point too. There are certain tips given for the avoidance of complications in Box 7.

CONCLUSION Complications in dermatosurgery office based-procedures although rare, do occur, and the outcomes of such events are related to the initial diagnosis and early management. Thorough preprocedural evaluation and identification of high-risk patients, 24 optimization of coexisting medical illness with medications will go a long way in preventing adverse events during the procedure. Good communication and patient rapport are important. Highrisk cases, technologically advanced procedures should be scheduled under monitored anesthesia care and in a hospital with full-fledged emergency backup facility. A well-planned and organized office setup under the leadership of a dermato­logist proves to be beneficial to the patients and reduce the medicolegal complications too.

## Episode Archive
It’s World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW) and we have prepared a special episode in light of that. In this episode of Communicable, Navaneeth Narayanan and Thomas Tängdén host Aula Abbara (London, UK), Guido Granata (Rome, Italy) and Tuomas Aro (Helsinki, Finland) to discuss the phenomenon of AMR in conflict and crisis zones. They elaborate on how difficult conditions and austere environments amplify the spread of AMR, drawing on findings from the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, Syria and other regions. Other topics covered include adapting antimicrobial stewardship and infection prevention and control (IPC) practices as well as the need for genuine political will and international collaboration to end conflicts and their exacerbation on AMR.
This episode follows the webinar “Beyond the frontlines” organised by ESCMID’s AMR Action Subcommittee for WAAW 2025, featuring the same guests, and is available on ESCMID Media. This Communicable episode was peer reviewed by Arjana Zerja of Mother Theresa University Hospital Centre, Tirana, Albania.

Once confined to the tropics, dengue is spreading via its vector, the _Aedes_ mosquito, to more temperate regions, causing increases in global morbidity, mortality and cost. In 2019, the WHO recognised dengue as one of the top ten global health threats alongside climate change and antimicrobial resistance [1]. In this episode of _Communicable_, Annie Joseph and Nav Narayanan welcome two dengue experts, André Siqueira of the non-profit Drugs for Neglected Diseases Initiative based in Geneva, Switzerland (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil), and Steven Lim of the Raja Permaisuri Bainun Hospital (Ipoh, Malaysia). Together, they discuss the epidemiology, clinical presentation and management of dengue including comparisons to other arboviral infections like zika and chikungunya, and the heightened risk of disease for vulnerable populations such as pregnant women and those with comorbidities. The conversation also highlights innovative vector-control strategies and candidate therapeutics currently under investigation.
This episode was edited by Kathryn Hostettler and peer reviewed by Loora Grünvald of the University of Tartu, Estonia.

In this episode of _Communicable_, Erin McCreary and Angela Huttner are joined by Barbara Trautner (St. Louis, USA) and Valéry Lavergne (Vancouver, Canada), the co-chairs and leading authors of the first IDSA guideline on complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI), which was published a few months ago [1]. Together, they discuss the process of developing the guideline from its conception in 2018, the new definition of cUTI, their stepwise approach to clinical decision-making, and some case-by-case scenarios for common antibiotics. They also elaborate on how this guideline compares (and contrasts) to other existing UTI guidelines—including the previous IDSA guideline for UTI [2] —and the clinical need to supply frontline clinicians to identify and distinguish complicated cases from the uncomplicated ones. The episode closes with what essential clinical questions the guests hope to tackle next.
This episode was edited by Kathryn Hostettler and peer reviewed by Maria Ana Flores of Santa Maria Local Health Unit, Lisbon, Portugal.

Contrary to popular belief, peer review has only recently been an integral step in scientific publishing. Currently seen by many as a badge of honour ensuring that published research is valid, innovative and honest, peer review seems in reality to be increasingly thankless, exploitative, and sometimes invisible. How did we get here? In this episode of _Communicable_, Annie Joseph and Angela Huttner are joined by two experts, Melinda Baldwin (University of Maryland, USA) and Serge Horbach (Radboud University, Netherlands), to unpack and examine the role of peer review, why it is still essential and how it fits within the greater editorial process. The conversation covers the history of peer review, contemporary formats including open review and the use of artificial intelligence, and thoughtful discussion on how to fix or rethink peer review.
This episode was edited by Kathryn Hostettler and peer reviewed by Barbora Píšová from the Czech Republic.

In this second-ever collaboration between SIDP’s _Breakpoints_ and ESCMID’s _Communicable_ podcasts, hosts Erin McCreary and Angela Huttner invite the two principal investigators and visionaries who spearheaded the Bacteraemia Antibiotic Length Actually Needed for Clinical Effectiveness (BALANCE) trial, Nick Daneman and Rob Fowler (Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, Toronto), for a “deep dive into all things that went into this trial” (1). The BALANCE trial spanned over ten years investigating - as the acronym title suggests - whether a shorter treatment duration of seven days was non-inferior to the standard of care of fourteen days for bacteraemia. The conversation covers everything from the initial hallway discussions that sparked the trial to the trial itself that screened over 36,000 patients and enrolled +3,600, its key takeaways and its impact on clinical practice as well as what’s next for Daneman and Fowler.

#### Episode 52 – Providing Care to Foreign-Born and Hard-to-Reach Individuals with Dr Carlos del Rio
In episode 52 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Carlos del Rio joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss the topic of providing care to foreign-born individuals. Dr del Rio is a Distinguished Professor of Medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at Emory University School of Medicine. He has held numerous positions at Emory University including as co-Director of the Emory Center for AIDS Research (CFAR) and co-PI of the Emory-CDC HIV Clinical Trials Unit and the Emory Vaccine and Treatment Evaluation Unit. He has worked more than a decade with hard-to-reach populations including people with substance use disorders to improve outcomes of those with HIV and to prevent infection with those at risk. Dr del Rio discusses steps his clinic has taken to provide care to hard-to-reach populations including understanding why patients miss appointments. Dr Saag and Dr del Rio also discuss the unique challenges that foreign-born individuals have in accessing care and the impact of current immigration enforcement on people in need of care and on the broader healthcare workforce. Dr del Rio shares his personal family history with immigration to illustrate the diverse nature of foreign-born people in the United States. Dr Saag and Dr del Rio close by emphasizing the need for clinicians to be passionate in providing care and compassion to their foreign-born patients at a time of immigration enforcement actions by federal authorities.
Listen >

#### Episode 51 – The Measles Outbreak and the Role Anti-Science Plays in Threatening Public Health with Dr Peter Hotez
In episode 51 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Peter Hotez joins host Dr Michael Saag to provide an update on the measles outbreak in the US and discuss the role that anti-science plays in threatening public health. Dr Hotez is a Professor of Pediatrics and Molecular Virology and Microbiology at Baylor College of Medicine. He is the author of more than 700 scientific papers and four books and is an ardent vaccine advocate and “science explainer” who combats anti-science and antisemitism in America, and globally. Dr Hotez and Dr Saag provide an overview of the current measles outbreak in the United States and the high rate of transmission. They discuss efforts to increase rates of vaccination, especially in a climate of misinformation about the safety and efficacy of the measles vaccine. Dr Saag and Dr Hotez discuss the origins of misinformation during the COVID-19 pandemic, including a discussion of the incentives of health and wellness influencers to spread false information. They also discuss how best to distribute accurate health information about vaccines on social media. They conclude by reviewing the successful history of childhood vaccination programs and the risk of future pandemics in a climate of disinformation about vaccination.
Listen >

#### Episode 50 – How Vaccines Get Approved in the US: The RSV Story and the Role of the ACIP – Dr Yvonne Maldonado
In episode 50 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Yvonne Maldonado joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine and the vaccine approval process in the United States. Dr Maldonado is a Professor in the Stanford University School of Medicine where she has achieved national and international recognition for her scholarship in the epidemiology and control of infectious diseases. She has served on several national and international committees including, until recently, the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). Dr Maldonado and Dr Saag provide an overview of RSV including the history of RSV vaccine research and development and provide an update on the availability of RSV vaccine in adults but not in children. They also discuss the risk of severe disease in children and the limited treatments available. Dr Maldonado and Dr Saag also discuss the process for vaccine approvals in the United States. Specifically, they review the role of the ACIP committee in vaccine approvals and provide an update on the recent dismissal of all of the prior members of the committee, which included Dr Maldonado. They discuss the potential impact that this will have on the review of all vaccines and the overall impact on public health.
Listen >

#### Episode 49 – Next-Gen HIV Prevention and Treatment, with Dr Judith Currier
In episode 49 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Judith Currier joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss _Next-Gen HIV Prevention and Treatment_. Dr Currier is a Professor of Medicine at UCLA and has more than 25 years of experience in the design, implementation, conduct, and analysis of clinical trials to optimize antiretroviral management of HIV and related complications. Dr Currier and Dr Saag provide an overview of why new antiretroviral drugs are needed and discuss the successful return on investment in biomedical research. They also provide a detailed review of long-acting antiretroviral drugs and discuss the state of current research for new options, including a discussion of lenacapavir. Finally, they share their concerns for what is at stake if attempts to cut the federal research budget are successful and the disruption it will bring to the progress that has been made in HIV care and other viral diseases.
Listen >

#### Episode 48 – Breaking the Silence: An Activist’s Approach, with Mary Fisher
In this episode of Going _anti_-Viral, Mary Fisher joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss _Communicating the Importance of Science and Research to the Public._ Ms Fisher is an artist, author, and activist, who has spent a lifetime giving voice to the voiceless. Her historic speech at the 1992 Republican Convention, _A Whisper of AIDS_, has been named one of “forty famous speeches that have had long-term effect on society.” In this episode, Ms Fisher discusses her history of activism including her work in Africa before and after the arrival of PEPFAR and the concern for the many communities she worked with given the termination of USAID. Ms Fisher also discusses her new book _Uneasy Silence: An activist seeks justice and courage over a lifetime of change_ where she and Dr Saag stress the importance of speaking out for scientific research given the impact it has on patient care and saving lives.
Listen >

#### Episode 47 – 40+ Years of HIV: What’s Changed, What Hasn’t, What Shouldn’t, What Must with Rebecca Denison
In this episode of Going _anti_-Viral, Rebecca Denison joins host Dr Michael Saag as a follow-up discussion to her Martin Delaney presentation at CROI 2025: 40+ Years of HIV: What’s Changed, What Hasn’t, What Shouldn’t, What Must. Ms Denison is an HIV-positive writer, educator, mother, and founder of WORLD, Women Organized to Respond to Life-threatening Diseases. Dr Saag and Ms Denison reflect on her history of living with HIV and her 40 + years as an HIV activist. They discuss the impact that recent cuts at USAID and PEPFAR are having international efforts to reduce HIV transmission and the loss in trust in healthcare practitioners since programs have been terminated. They also discuss concerns about cuts to federal funding for HIV care programs in the US and the impact of recent loss of staff expertise at federal agencies. Finally, Dr Saag and Ms Denison ask all care clinicians to share their stories to their communities as a way of becoming advocates for the importance of HIV care.

#### Episode 46 – Development of a Hepatitis C Cure with Dr Raymond Schinazi
In this episode of Going _Anti-_ Viral, Dr Raymond Schinazi joins host Dr Michael Saag for an in-depth conversation about the development of a cure for hepatitis C. Dr Schinazi, the Frances Winship Walters Professor of Pediatrics and Director of the Laboratory of Biochemical Pharmacology at Emory University, shares insights from his distinguished career in antiviral research and development. He begins by outlining his background and long-standing interest in antiviral therapies, including groundbreaking work in HIV treatment. The conversation then shifts to his pivotal role in the development of sofosbuvir, a breakthrough direct-acting antiviral drug in the cure for hepatitis C, and the importance of NS5A inhibitors in antiviral drug regimens. Dr Schinazi also offers a rare behind-the-scenes look at the business and regulatory journey of bringing a transformative therapy to market, reflecting on the personal impact of this milestone. The episode concludes with a discussion of his current research into potential treatments for hepatitis B.

#### Episode 45 – Bacteriophages for the Treatment of Antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) Bacterial Infections with Dr Graham F. Hatfull
In this episode of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Michael Saag speaks with Dr Graham Hatfull, a Professor of Biological Sciences at the University of Pittsburgh.Dr Hatfull joins Dr Saag to discuss**_Bacteriophages for the treatment of antimicrobial-resistant (AMR) bacterial infections_**. Dr Hatfull provides an overview of the types of bacteriophages and how they can be used to treat antimicrobial-resistant bacteria. Dr Hatfull and Dr Saag discuss the challenges of treating bacterial infections with phages, given the diversity and complexity of the different types of bacteria, and bringing phage treatments to scale. Finally, they discuss what future research is needed to overcome the challenges of phage treatment and look to the future where technology enables synthetically produced phages to provide targeted therapy to antimicrobial resistant bacteria.

#### Episode 44 – IAS–USA 2025 Update of the Drug Resistance Mutations in HIV-1 with Dr Annemarie M. Wensing
In this episode of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Michael Saag speaks with Dr Annemarie M. Wensing, a Clinical Virologist at the University Medical Center Utrecht and an Honorary Professor at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. Dr Wensing joins Dr Saag to discuss the recently released**_IAS–USA 2025 Update of the Drug Resistance Mutations in HIV-1_**. Dr Wensing discusses the influence of Dr Charles Boucher in developing her interest in the topic of HIV drug resistance and Dr Wensing and Dr Saag provide an overview of HIV drug resistance and testing. Dr Wensing also provides advice to clinicians on how to manage patients who experience drug resistance.Dr Wensing and Dr Saag then discuss an upcoming report soon to be published that addresses the potential role and the important limitations of HIV DNA resistance testing. Finally, they address the topic of drug resistance in the absence of resistance mutations and look ahead to what the future holds for the field of HIV resistance.
A current list of mutations associated with clinical resistance to HIV and the accompanying user notes, regularly revised and disseminated by the IAS–USA Drug Resistance Mutations Group, were published in _Topics in Antiviral Medicine_™ on March 4, 2025. The figures are also available as downloadable PDFand PowerPoint Slides.

#### Episode 43 – Innovations in HIV Service Delivery: Building a Path Forward with Those Left Behind with Dr Izukanji Sikazwe
In this episode of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Michael Saag speaks with Dr Izukanji Sikazwe, the Chief Executive Officer for the Centre for Infectious Disease Research in Zambia (CIDRZ). Dr Sikazwe joins Dr Saag to provide an overview of her symposium presentation at the 2025 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) entitled **_Innovations in HIV Service Delivery: Building a Path Forward with Those Left Behind_**. Dr Sikazwe discusses her career journey in treatment of HIV in Zambia and her path to CIDRZ. Dr Sikazwe and Dr Saag discuss the history of HIV and AIDS in Zambia and address the impact that PEPFAR had on the disease when it arrived in the country in 2004. They discuss how PEPFAR has operated in Zambia and provide a current overview of the sudden cancellation of USAID contracts on those receiving HIV care and treatment and other health services. Finally, they look ahead given the current disruptions on how Zambia and other countries can move forward to meet the needs of those in need of care.

#### Episode 41 - Meeting the Treatment and Prevention Needs of Transgender Women with Dr Tonia Poteat
In this episode of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Michael Saag speaks with Dr Tonia Poteat, a professor in the Duke University School of Nursing and co-director of the Duke SGM Wellness Program. Dr Poteat joins Dr Saag to provide an overview of a Themed Discussion session that she is leading at CROI 2025 entitled _Meeting the Treatment and Prevention Needs of Transgender Women_. Dr Poteat and Dr Saag address the 3 most common challenges faced in the care of transgender persons: uninformed clinicians, societal discrimination, and efforts by some state governments and the federal government to limit the rights of transgender persons. They discuss efforts to educate clinicians and summarize the resources that are available to clinicians to help provide care to transgender persons facing stigma and discrimination. They also discuss efforts in the judicial system to take legal action against discriminatory policies of state and federal governments. Dr Poteat also provides an overview of the presentations discussed at the Themed Discussion session that she is leading at CROI 2025 on Monday March 11, 2025. Finally, Dr Poteat and Dr Saag look ahead to the next five years of transgender care and provide advice to all involved in the care of transgender persons during a challenging time.

#### Episode 40 - HIV Cure Research: State of the Art and Navigating Presentations at CROI 2025 with Dr Joseph J. Eron, Jr
In this episode of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Michael Saag speaks with Dr Joseph Eron, Professor of Medicine at University of North Carolina (UNC) about the topic of his upcoming presentation at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) 2025: _HIV Cure Research: State of the Art and Navigating Presentations at CROI 2025_. Dr Eron discusses the state of HIV cure research including a detailed discussion of why it has been so difficult to develop a cure for HIV. Dr Saag and Dr Eron discuss the difference between HIV cure and functional cure and provide a detailed overview of cure research efforts looking at blocking and locking HIV in human DNA. Dr Saag and Dr Eron also discuss the potential for “molecular scissors” (CRISPR-Cas9) to cure HIV. Finally, they provide an overview of cure research that will be presented at CROI, highlighting the plenary presentation by Dr Ole Søgaard at CROI on Monday March 10 entitled _HIV Cure: A Translational Research Perspective._ For more information about the topic of this episode, listen to an earlier episode of Going _anti_-Viral where Dr Saag discusses Vaccine Development with Dr Richard Koup, see links in the resources below.

#### Episode 39 - Preview of 2025 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) with Dr Diane V. Havlir

Dr Havlir currently serves as Chair of the Scientific Program Committee for the 2025 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) and joins Dr Saag to provide a preview of CROI 2025. #### Episode 72 - Neurodegeneration and Dementia Risk in Older Adults with HIV: Biomarkers and Epidemiology with Dr Alan Winston (March 24, 2026)

#### Episode 70 - From Wall Street to ACT UP: A Life Rewritten by HIV with Peter Staley (February 27, 2026)

#### Episode 69 - Successes in HIV-1 Vaccine Design: Accelerating Completion of One of Sciences’ Most Difficult Vaccines with Dr Kevin Saunders (February 25, 2026)

#### Episode 67 - Reflections on a Career of HIV Medicine, Mentorship, and Scientific Legacy with Dr Martin S. Hirsch (February 10, 2026)
In episode 67 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Martin Hirsch joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss his career in HIV medicine, mentorship, and his scientific legacy.Dr Hirsch is a Professor Emeritus at Harvard Medical School and was Director of the Harvard Collaborative AIDS Treatment Evaluation Unit from 1986 to 2003 and Director of the Harvard Multidisciplinary AIDS Research Training Grant. Dr Hirsch’s research focused on finding drug combinations that delay the development of multidrug resistance and reduce viral replication in HIV-1 infection. Dr Hirsch served as an Editorial Board member for numerous prestigious medical journals over the past 3 decades, including AIDS,the _New England Journal of Medicine_,_Clinical Infectious Diseases_, and the _Journal of Infectious Diseases_,where he was Editor-in-Chief. Dr Hirsch discusses his extensive career, the evolution of antiviral therapies, and the importance of mentorship in science. He reflects on his early experiences, the emergence of HIV, and the collaborative efforts that led to advancements in treatment. Dr Hirsch emphasizes the need for individualized mentorship and shares insights on the future of HIV research and his optimism for the potential of HIV prophylactic treatments.
Listen >

#### Episode 66 - Preview of the 2026 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI) – Dr Nicolas Chomont (January 27, 2026)
In episode 66 of Going anti-Viral, Dr Nicolas Chomont joins host Dr Michael Saag to provide a preview of the 2026 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections (CROI). Dr Chomont is Chair of the Scientific Program Committee for CROI 2026 and is a Professor in the Department of Microbiology, Infectious Diseases, and Immunology at the Université de Montréal and a researcher at the CHUM Research Centre. Dr Chomont discusses CROI 2026, highlighting its significance in advancing HIV research and treatment. He emphasizes the importance of community engagement, the support for new investigators, and ongoing research for an HIV cure. The discussion provides the overall themes of the abstracts accepted for CROI 2026 as well as the plenary sessions, symposia, and the impact of funding cuts on research and treatment. Dr Chomont expresses optimism about the future of HIV research and the collaborative spirit of the conference.
Listen >

#### Episode 65 – IAS-USA Lifetime of Leadership Award – Dr Gerald Friedland (January 13, 2026)
In episode 65 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Gerald Friedland joins host Dr Michael Saag as the recipient of the IAS–USA Lifetime of Leadership Award, established nearly 15 years ago to honor individuals whose contributions have left a profound and lasting impact on HIV medicine, scientific education, and the mission of the IAS–USA. Dr Friedland discusses his extensive journey in the field of HIV/AIDS and infectious diseases, reflecting on his early career, the challenges faced during the early years of the AIDS epidemic, and the evolution of treatment strategies. Dr Friedland and Dr Saag emphasize the importance of collaboration, compassion, and the pursuit of knowledge in addressing public health crises. Dr Friedland also discusses his research on tuberculosis and the integration of HIV treatment, highlighting important findings that have impacted healthcare practices.
Listen >

#### Episode 63 – The Role of Outcomes Research on Clinical Decisions for Patient Care with Dr Mari Kitahata (December 16, 2025)
In episode 63 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Mari Kitahata joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss the role of outcomes research on clinical decisions for patient care. Dr Kitahata is a Professor of Medicine at the University of Washington (UW) in the Division of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. For more than 3 decades, she has directed the UW/Fred Hutch Center for AIDS Research (CFAR) Clinical Research Core. Dr Kitahata’s research focuses on improving long-term outcomes for people with HIV and she has led studies demonstrating key determinants of increased survival in people with HIV, including early initiation of antiretroviral therapy and care managed by physicians with greater HIV experience. Dr Kitahata discusses the significance of outcomes research in clinical settings, particularly in the context of HIV care. She explains the differences between efficacy and effectiveness, the challenges faced in observational studies, and the importance of statistical techniques to address biases. Dr Kitahata and Dr Saag discuss the role of electronic medical records (EMRs) in enhancing data collection and the necessity of data validation through adjudication processes. Additionally, the conversation touches on the importance of patient-reported outcomes and the limitations of EMR data, including issues of misclassification. Finally, Dr Saag and Dr Kitahata discuss the distinction between predictive modeling and etiologic modeling in research, underscoring the complexities of clinical care and the future directions for outcomes research.
Listen >

#### Episode 62 – The COVID-19 Pandemic and the Current State of Public Health in the US with Dr Rochelle Walensky (December 2, 2025)
In episode 62 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Rochelle Walensky joins host Dr Michael Saag on World AIDS Day 2025 to discuss her experience as the Director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) during the COVID-19 pandemic and the current state of public health in the United States. Dr Walensky is a Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School and has published over 300 research articles that have motivated changes to US HIV testing and immigration policy and promoted expanded funding for HIV-related research, treatment, and the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR). Dr Walensky reflects on her experience during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic in Massachusetts, where she was the Chief of the Division of Infectious Diseases at Massachusetts General Hospital. Dr Saag and Dr Walensky then discuss her transition to the Director of the CDC and her management of the agency during the pandemic. Dr Walensky and Dr Saag emphasize the dedication of public health professionals and the need for continued support and understanding of the challenges they face. They discuss the risk of proposed budget cuts to the CDC and the impacts this will have on the agency as well as state and local public health departments. Finally, they discuss the future of public health and their shared optimism for public health over the long-term.
Listen >

#### Episode 61 – The Evidence for Vaccine Safety and Effectiveness with Dr Yvonne Maldonado (November 18, 2025)
In episode 61 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Yvonne Maldonado joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss the evidence for vaccine safety and effectiveness. Dr Maldonado is a Professor in the Stanford University School of Medicine where she has achieved national and international recognition for her scholarship in the epidemiology and control of infectious diseases. She has served on several national and international committees including, until recently, the CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP).Dr Maldonado and Dr Saag provide an overview of how vaccines work and discuss where aluminum adjuvants are used in vaccines and address the validity of “anti-vax” claims about the use of aluminum in vaccines. Dr Maldonado emphasizes the crucial role of vaccination, particularly the measles vaccine, as a key indicator of public health and discusses the high infectiousness of measles and its implications for community safety, especially for children and immunocompromised individuals. Dr Maldonado advocates for a social contract where individuals take responsibility for the health of others through vaccination, highlighting the need for well-planned immunization schedules. Dr Saag and Dr Maldonado also discuss current recommendations for the COVID-19 vaccine, its safety, and whether pregnant women and infants should receive the vaccine. Finally, Dr Saag and Dr Maldonado discuss the work of public health in the future and the importance of communicating the safety and effectiveness of vaccines.
Listen >

#### Episode 60 – Medical Cannabis: Evidence and Insight with Dr Donald Abrams (November 4, 2025)
In episode 60 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Donald Abrams joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss medical cannabis. Dr Abrams is a professor emeritus at the University of California San Francisco and a specialist in integrative oncology at the Osher Center for Integrative Health. Dr Abrams has studied complementary and alternative therapies, including mind-body treatments, botanical therapies, medical use of cannabis, and herbal therapies used in traditional Chinese medicine. He continues to research the health effects of medical cannabis. Dr Abrams was previously at the forefront of HIV/AIDS research and treatment at San Francisco General Hospital and served as chief of the medical oncology service from 2003 to 2017. Dr Saag and Dr Abrams discuss the history of medical cannabis and the challenges Dr Abrams experienced in researching its use for medical therapy. They discuss the medical benefits of cannabis and the recommendations that clinicians may make, as well as addressing the differences in products available, including THC and CBD. They also discuss research on whether the use of cannabis in young adults is related to schizophrenia. Finally, Dr Saag and Dr Abrams discuss the future of medical cannabis and whether physicians should continue to provide a role in its use, whether the scheduling of cannabis as a controlled substance will change, and the type of research that is needed to continue to explore where its use is beneficial.
Listen >

#### Episode 59 – The CDC without Scientific Leadership with Dr Demetre Daskalakis (October 21, 2025)
In episode 59 of Going _anti_-Viral,Dr Demetre Daskalakis joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss his career in public health and the turnover in leadership at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).Dr Daskalakis is an infectious diseases physician who served in leadership roles at the CDC from 2020 to 2025. He was director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases and was previously director of the Division of HIV Prevention at the National Center for HIV/AIDS, Viral Hepatitis, STD, and TB Prevention. In 2022, he was appointed deputy coordinator of the White House response to the mpox outbreak. Dr Daskalakis discusses his career in public health and leadership roles in infectious diseases. Dr Saag and Dr Daskalakis have a detailed discussion about applying lessons learned from the HIV epidemic in the national response to the mpox outbreak and they discuss Dr Daskalakis’s role at the CDC in response to the current measles outbreak. They also address ideologic-driven changes at the CDC under the direction of Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr. and the Department of Health and Human Services including the firing of Dr Susan Monarez and Dr Daskalakis’ subsequent resignation. Finally, they discuss the current direction of the CDC and the outlook for public health without scientific leadership.They also discuss the possibility of a renaissance for public health in the future where it can be reimagined to focus on people instead of historic funding paradigms.
Listen >

#### Episode 58 – Demystifying Syphilis: Diagnosis and Treatment with Khalil Ghanem (October 7, 2025)
In episode 58 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Khalil Ghanem joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss current challenges in the diagnosis and treatment of syphilis. Dr Ghanem is a Professor of Medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine. Dr Ghanem’s research focuses on reproductive tract infections in particular syphilis and the vaginal microbiome. He was a consultant to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on the development of the 2010 and 2015 Adult Syphilis Treatment Guidelines. Dr Ghanem discusses the history and current trends of syphilis, including the impact of doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (DoxyPEP) on infection rates. Dr Saag and Dr Ghanem also address screening and testing for syphilis and the current issues faced in diagnosis and treatment including the management of penicillin G benzathine shortages. Finally, Dr Ghanem looks ahead to new research to address syphilis management, emphasizing the need for better diagnostics and treatment options, especially during pregnancy..
Listen >

## Episode Archive
It’s World AMR Awareness Week (WAAW) and we have prepared a special episode in light of that. In this episode of Communicable, Navaneeth Narayanan and Thomas Tängdén host Aula Abbara (London, UK), Guido Granata (Rome, Italy) and Tuomas Aro (Helsinki, Finland) to discuss the phenomenon of AMR in conflict and crisis zones. They elaborate on how difficult conditions and austere environments amplify the spread of AMR, drawing on findings from the ongoing conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza, Syria and other regions. Other topics covered include adapting antimicrobial stewardship and infection prevention and control (IPC) practices as well as the need for genuine political will and international collaboration to end conflicts and their exacerbation on AMR.
This episode follows the webinar “Beyond the frontlines” organised by ESCMID’s AMR Action Subcommittee for WAAW 2025, featuring the same guests, and is available on ESCMID Media. This Communicable episode was peer reviewed by Arjana Zerja of Mother Theresa University Hospital Centre, Tirana, Albania.

Once confined to the tropics, dengue is spreading via its vector, the _Aedes_ mosquito, to more temperate regions, causing increases in global morbidity, mortality and cost. In 2019, the WHO recognised dengue as one of the top ten global health threats alongside climate change and antimicrobial resistance [1]. In this episode of _Communicable_, Annie Joseph and Nav Narayanan welcome two dengue experts, André Siqueira of the non-profit Drugs for Neglected Diseases Initiative based in Geneva, Switzerland (Rio de Janeiro, Brazil), and Steven Lim of the Raja Permaisuri Bainun Hospital (Ipoh, Malaysia). Together, they discuss the epidemiology, clinical presentation and management of dengue including comparisons to other arboviral infections like zika and chikungunya, and the heightened risk of disease for vulnerable populations such as pregnant women and those with comorbidities. The conversation also highlights innovative vector-control strategies and candidate therapeutics currently under investigation.
This episode was edited by Kathryn Hostettler and peer reviewed by Loora Grünvald of the University of Tartu, Estonia.

## Episode Archive
In this episode of _Communicable_, Erin McCreary and Angela Huttner are joined by Barbara Trautner (St. Louis, USA) and Valéry Lavergne (Vancouver, Canada), the co-chairs and leading authors of the first IDSA guideline on complicated urinary tract infection (cUTI), which was published a few months ago [1]. Together, they discuss the process of developing the guideline from its conception in 2018, the new definition of cUTI, their stepwise approach to clinical decision-making, and some case-by-case scenarios for common antibiotics. They also elaborate on how this guideline compares (and contrasts) to other existing UTI guidelines—including the previous IDSA guideline for UTI [2] —and the clinical need to supply frontline clinicians to identify and distinguish complicated cases from the uncomplicated ones. The episode closes with what essential clinical questions the guests hope to tackle next.
This episode was edited by Kathryn Hostettler and peer reviewed by Maria Ana Flores of Santa Maria Local Health Unit, Lisbon, Portugal.
**Listen on your favourite channel**
Contrary to popular belief, peer review has only recently been an integral step in scientific publishing. Currently seen by many as a badge of honour ensuring that published research is valid, innovative and honest, peer review seems in reality to be increasingly thankless, exploitative, and sometimes invisible. How did we get here? In this episode of _Communicable_, Annie Joseph and Angela Huttner are joined by two experts, Melinda Baldwin (University of Maryland, USA) and Serge Horbach (Radboud University, Netherlands), to unpack and examine the role of peer review, why it is still essential and how it fits within the greater editorial process. The conversation covers the history of peer review, contemporary formats including open review and the use of artificial intelligence, and thoughtful discussion on how to fix or rethink peer review.
This episode was edited by Kathryn Hostettler and peer reviewed by Barbora Píšová from the Czech Republic.

## Episode Archive
In this second-ever collaboration between SIDP’s _Breakpoints_ and ESCMID’s _Communicable_ podcasts, hosts Erin McCreary and Angela Huttner invite the two principal investigators and visionaries who spearheaded the Bacteraemia Antibiotic Length Actually Needed for Clinical Effectiveness (BALANCE) trial, Nick Daneman and Rob Fowler (Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, Toronto), for a “deep dive into all things that went into this trial” (1). The BALANCE trial spanned over ten years investigating - as the acronym title suggests - whether a shorter treatment duration of seven days was non-inferior to the standard of care of fourteen days for bacteraemia. The conversation covers everything from the initial hallway discussions that sparked the trial to the trial itself that screened over 36,000 patients and enrolled +3,600, its key takeaways and its impact on clinical practice as well as what’s next for Daneman and Fowler.
This episode was edited by Kathryn Hostettler and Megan Klatt, and peer reviewed by Dr. Arjana Zerja of Mother Theresa University Hospital Centre, Tirana, Albania.

#### Episode 52 – Providing Care to Foreign-Born and Hard-to-Reach Individuals with Dr Carlos del Rio
In episode 52 of Going _anti_-Viral, Dr Carlos del Rio joins host Dr Michael Saag to discuss the topic of providing care to foreign-born individuals. Dr del Rio is a Distinguished Professor of Medicine in the Division of Infectious Diseases at Emory University School of Medicine. He has held numerous positions at Emory University including as co-Director of the Emory Center for AIDS Research (CFAR) and co-PI of the Emory-CDC HIV Clinical Trials Unit and the Emory Vaccine and Treatment Evaluation Unit. He has worked more than a decade with hard-to-reach populations including people with substance use disorders to improve outcomes of those with HIV and to prevent infection with those at risk. Dr del Rio discusses steps his clinic has taken to provide care to hard-to-reach populations including understanding why patients miss appointments. Dr Saag and Dr del Rio also discuss the unique challenges that foreign-born individuals have in accessing care and the impact of current immigration enforcement on people in need of care and on the broader healthcare workforce. Dr del Rio shares his personal family history with immigration to illustrate the diverse nature of foreign-born people in the United States. Dr Saag and Dr del Rio close by emphasizing the need for clinicians to be passionate in providing care and compassion to their foreign-born patients at a time of immigration enforcement actions by federal authorities.
Listen >
